The central focus remains on using these ML-based controllers to improve stability and extend the operational lifespan of NCPS, which are typically composed of multiple interconnected microgrids. Specifically, the research highlights applications in stability analysis and control enhancement, including the management of active and reactive power, frequency regulation, and voltage stability across individual microgrids and the overall system. Finally, the study includes a tabular summary of various ML applications within modern control theory and concludes with an overview of both current challenges and future research directions.

During the last few decades, numerous studies have been dedicated to unraveling the origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess components in blazar spectra. While various mechanisms have been proposed to explain these features, a consensus favors inverse Compton scattering as the physical process responsible. A critical point of contention remains whether the targets are the broad-line region (BLR) clouds or the external photon fields originating from the host galaxy. This study introduces a novel Monte Carlo algorithm, MAPPIES, designed to generate spectrum-based models of active galactic nuclei (AGN) that remain consistent with the external Compton (IC) scenario. A distinct advantage of MAPPIES is its relaxation of prior constraints regarding target properties; the inputs required for the models are the observed spectral data themselves, and no initial assumptions regarding the targets are pre-decided. Instead, both the probabilities and characteristics of the absorbing/given environments are derived directly from fitting the external Compton component to the dataset. To validate this methodology, we applied MAPPIES to analyze three well-documented blazar spectra, and the resulting models successfully replicate the spectral features while offering clear evidence that the soft X-ray excess in each case arises entirely from inverse Compton scattering of host galaxy photons.

This study addresses the challenge of forecasting time-based data across multiple consecutive periods, such as daily sales volumes, weekly energy usage, or monthly housing costs. We propose a novel hierarchical model that effectively captures the multi-period sequence while also accounting for missing values. The method utilizes a recurrent network architecture designed to model temporal dependencies between successive forecasts. To enhance the model's efficiency and adaptability, we introduce a Bayesian approach that automatically learns the most informative previous forecasts and discards less relevant ones. This adaptation is achieved by employing a Gaussian mixture distribution over selected features of the multi-period time series. We derive the full set of full posterior distributions for all latent variables and model parameters in closed form. The resulting analytical posterior updates enable efficient convergence to an optimal solution using the coordinate ascent Laplace approximation technique. Empirical results demonstrate that our method effectively handles complex, multi-period series and outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and robustness.

We investigate a unified model that connects the leptogenesis and dark energy sectors by assuming a direct link between the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the dark energy field and the total lepton number. In this framework, dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of the universe, while leptagenic processes generate the baryon asymmetry of the cosmos. We demonstrate that because of this proposed coupling, variations in the baryon asymmetry directly influence both magnitude of dark energy and its equation of state. Furthermore, we establish that this interdependence allows for the determination of the baryon asymmetry through observational cosmological data.

We introduce a learning-based controller designed to master locomotion across four environments—swimming in 2D fluid, walking on land, flying in 3D—using only limited data and auxiliary information. Our method relies on training a regression model to transform this side information into action parameters for Gaussian mixture action sets, where the number of training samples is intentionally restricted to expose the algorithm to noise, uncertainty, and modeling errors. To guarantee stability despite these imperfections, we establish theoretical conditions by integrating data-driven control with Lyapunov-based analysis. We validate the proposed approach using training data sets that lack walking or flight modes, yet the resulting controller successfully learns all four behaviors, even achieving all-six 3D land locomotion and 3D flight capabilities. The proposed framework is implemented within the open-source Multi-bi-physic Simulation Environment (MUSE).

By applying generation models to stored semantic traits, these results demonstrate competitive performance across multiple benchmarks, thereby validating the effectiveness of this proposed framework.

Current lexical object detection (LexOD) methods rely on training with fixed, closed sets of object categories. Consequently, the inability to leverage novel classes during detection necessitates laborious manual annotation when encountering new objects. To address this limitation, this work introduces an open LexOD framework utilizing pseudo bounding-box annotations. By generating class-specific predictions to derive these pseudo bounding boxes, the model facilitates annotations derived directly from the detection system. Evaluating this approach on two public datasets demonstrates that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models, effectively balancing detection accuracy with experimental results showing the system handles an unlimited lexicon of object classes without requiring fixed pre-defined output categories.

The PDR in Rho Ophiuchus is a unique system allowing the dispersion properties of atomic, ionized, and molecular gas to be examined independently. This study investigates the spatial distribution and velocity structure of the PDR, as well as the dispersion characteristics of atomic and ionized components, by utilizing 13CO and CII emission data obtained from the ALMA telescope. We employed a novel technique involving the estimation of the velocity dispersion profile and its radial dependence across a specific source region. Our findings indicate that the atomic gas in the PDR is dispersed similarly to molecular gas, and unlike findings from previous studies, the velocity profiles reveal no significant rotation. Furthermore, we modeled the CII emission source to determine its size, resulting in findings that closely align with the spatial extent of the 13CO emission. This suggests that ionized gas is effectively distributed throughout PDR regions, a result consistent with earlier observations regarding the atomic components. Finally, we discuss these results alongside the existing model of the PDR in Rho Ophiuchus proposed by K. Schilke et al. (2015).

This study addresses the challenge of forecasting short-term mortality rates, particularly for older demographics where volatility and irregular patterns are prominent. We propose an enhanced out-of-sample prediction framework based on Gaussian factor models, incorporating time-varying loadings modeled through Markov chain switching mechanisms to capture structural shifts. First, we detail the statistical inference procedure for estimating model parameters, including state trajectories; subsequently, we apply the framework to generate mortality forecasts. The forecast accuracy of this novel, time-dependent approach is evaluated and contrasted against benchmarks relying on constant mortality factors. Results from simulations and empirical analysis demonstrate the time-varying model's superior predictive performance. Furthermore, evidence suggests a time-allowed time-dependent model is more effective than one assuming time-invariance, notably improving reliability when projecting long-term mortality for reaching advanced ages.

Neuroevolutionary approaches have become a standard for model selection in machine learning, yet search strategies often suffer from suboptimal resource allocation due to inefficient substructure recombination. These strategies struggle to locate optimal substructures within a diffusive search space, which leads to excessive training costs and delays convergence. This paper investigates substructure interference—a phenomenon where conflicting substructures hinder search performance—and proposes a solution by employing a shared training strategy to mitigate interference among substructures. Experimental results across multiple architectures demonstrate that this approach improves search efficiency by up to 30% while surpassing prior state-of-the-art methods using both classical evolutionary algorithms and reinforcement learning frameworks.

Translator dependence represents a vital metric for assessing the quality of a translator's work; however, current methods to calculate it are both intricate and insufficient. Its implementation relies on established Bayesian estimation techniques, which have historically proven effective in generating reliable estimations of unknown parameters from sampled data sets. This paper investigates the implications of removing invalid or unconnected weights in training deep learning models. It first demonstrates that the trimmed learning approach significantly accelerates both Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Fully-Connected Neural Networks (FCNs) without compromising their predictive accuracy. Subsequently, the study explores the optimal strategy for selecting the indices of the retained weights and positions of the deleted weights. Contrary to previous research, we prove that using convolutional structures to filter weights yields superior performance over random selection for both model types. Furthermore, the experiments reveal that the trimmed fully-connected network can be visualized as a collection of sparsely active, convolutional-like filters. These findings not only speed up the training of standard networks, rendering large-scale training more efficient, but also offer valuable theoretical insights into the success of modern deep learning paradigms.

We present the construction of a $\phi^Q$ operator with an anomalous dimension $\gamma_Q$ for even integers $Q \geq 6$ within perturbative calculations of $Q\phi$ interactions in $d = 6 - \epsilon$ dimensions for an $O(N)$-symmetric theory. This theory describes $N$ real scalar fields interacting via $\lambda \phi^Q / Q$ at six loops, and the study focuses on the fixed-point value of $\gamma_Q$ at two loops. We also examine the possibility that such operators with integer even $Q$ could be used to construct a Wilson-Fisher-type operator product expansion.

While the study of valley physics in two-dimensional (2D) materials has largely centered on electronic mechanisms, influence from phonons has historically been considered negligible. Using time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT), this work reveals phonon effects on valley dynamics in monolayer graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides. The research demonstrates exciton dephasing via distinct electron-inholographic phonon interactions in these systems: in graphene, electronic dispersion changes drive the process through interactions with in-plane phonons, whereas transition metal dichalcene occurs via coupling between the electron-holone wavefunction and out-of-plane phonons. Consequently, the rate of exciton dephasing in transition metal dichene is significantly faster than in monolayer graphene under comparable conditions.

The Visual Domain Adaptation (VDA) Challenge of NeurIPS 2022 evaluated approaches to various forms of VDA, including unsupervised, multi-unsupervised, and transductive scenarios. To address these challenges, this winning solution leverages a pre-trained vision transformer as a robust feature extractor, employing it alongside multiple auxiliary strategies such as label-distribution matching, entropy minimization, and pseudo-labeling. By integrating these components and performing separate optimizations for each VDA task specific to the contest, the approach achieved state-of-the-art results on the multi-unsupervised VDA task and set new performance benchmarks on the transductive VDA task.

T-Distributed Neighborhood Embedding (SNE) is a highly effective technique for large-scale visual data embedding. Nevertheless, it is constrained to Euclidean spaces and cannot represent data within a spherical manifold, even though much of the existing information exists in this format. To bridge this gap, we propose a manifold version of k-nearest neighbors-based spherical visualization (VMF SNE). Our method integrates three core components: representing data through a spherical distribution model to extract mean vectors and concentration matrices, calculating spherical distances to identify nearest neighbors, and applying the t-distribution for embedding visualization. To mitigate issues such as vanishing gradients, our model incorporates directional and tensorial convolution layers. To validate the approach, we conducted extensive experiments on major spherical datasets, including object recognition on MNIST, face analysis on LBF, and infrared recognition on LBF. The results demonstrate that VMF SNE outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Although uniform expansions converge more rapidly at moderate coupling, harmonic and exponential variants demonstrate superior accuracy under weak-coupling conditions where they significantly outperform uniform series. After accounting for underlying series divergences, we perform a combined DMC and analyticical resummation analysis, which yields a result for the ratio $m^*/m$ showing excellent alignment across all coupling regimes. Notably, this combined method also captures recent experimental findings by the group of D.S. Deacon (Science 376, 1189 (2023)), accurately determining the transition from a plus to a minus first-order energy branch at the polaron saturation coupling ($g_c$). Furthermore, our findings underscore that encompassing a broader spectrum of in-cuts in the perturbation series substantially enhances the convergence speed of uniform series expansions.

The widespread adoption of scrum has sparked significant interest regarding how remote work impacts software development. Although the benefits of a distributed, cost-effective, global talent pool are well-documented, research into the effects of fully remote environments on team dynamics and productivity remains limited. Consequently, this study seeks to address these gaps by investigating the influence of fully remote work on the performance and success of scrum projects. Employing a multi-method research design, the investigation utilizes an initial survey of 102 scrum teams, followed by a case study of a remote distributed team. The findings indicate that telecommuting significantly enhances the success of scrum projects, driven primarily by improved communication, more frequent interactions, and greater psychological safety. This remote capability also fosters stronger professional and personal relationships, thereby boosting productivity. Furthermore, the study offers practical implications and a framework for managers aiming to successfully integrate remote work into their projects.

This paper extends the definition to cover four by four and chosen vector-shaped non-negative matrices, while also deriving their associated Gaussian-Qu (Gau-Wu) values. By applying this extended definition to these two matrix categories, the study derives explicit formulas for their Gau-Wu values. The resulting theorems demonstrate that the scalar result previously established by Gau and Wu holds a broader, matricial interpretation.

The analysis utilizes data from the ALICE detector at the LHC, specifically isolating beauty contributions from non-prompt resonance decays. The physics potential of non-prompt resonance decays is further evaluated. In an extended theoretical investigation, the measured flow $v_2(p_{\rm T})$ is fitted using the core-crown model, interpreting the core component as arising from the hadronization of the initial quark distribution.

This paper establishes that for a $K$-user interference network, the gap between sum GDoF achieved through optimal continuous power allocation and binary (zero-forcing-like) power cutoff strategies scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. We derive precise cutoff thresholds for link signal-to-noise ratios that determine when shortening links should be deactivated. Under the binary approach using these thresholds and restricting transmission to active links via cutoffs, we provide sufficient conditions under which every link operates as specified by the threshold, thereby proving the overall binary power allocation is optimal and yielding a achievable sum GDoF lower bound. The core technical innovation involves a bound tightening method applied to the Chernoff bound on incomplete Gamma functions; this technique is not only instrumental in establishing the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit gap but also holds independent value as a methodological tool.

Internal audit serves as a crucial mechanism for organizations to mitigate risks and resolve issues, while also providing a reliable avenue for management decision-making. The expanding volume and complexity of data in internal auditing have created a pressing need for effective auditing techniques that can accurately classify audit units. This paper proposes a novel adaptive classification method that builds an initial training model and refines it adaptively as new data emerges. The underlying approach combines formal concept 2- 3-D and the 3-D theorems to generate evidence for class auditing objects. Empirical evidence demonstrates the superiority of this proposed adaptive 3-D algorithm over the adaptive 3-D weighted version model in classification accuracy tasks.

This work examines a framework where Deformed Special Relativity (DSR) emerges from a modified Heisenberg algebra influenced by the Planck scale. Within this structure, space and time remain standard under Galilean transformations but undergo deformation during Lorentz transformations. The analysis centers on identifying the specific deformation, denoted as $f(v)$, that maintains consistency between the planar commutation relations of coordinates and the three-dimensional algebra of planar positions and momenta. Furthermore, the study explores the physical implications of these deformations, offering insights into how fundamental scales and space-time symmetries are interconnected.

School schedules can be constructed to accommodate shared processing power, enabling schools to open their doors during the day as an educational facility for adult learners. This section formalizes the school timetable problem to incorporate adult education requirements and investigates the application of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulations utilizing the binary decision variables to manage scheduling constraints. This approach for both primary and secondary education is applied within the framework of a school timetable generator, which incorporates algorithms to manage shared computing resources; this research subsequently evaluates the computational performance of the generated timetables based on the characteristics of the input data. This study demonstrates how a school timetable can be created to host programs for both children and adults.

The formulation of the school timetable can be created to accommodate shared adult education programs, which requires a school to close its doors during the day. This section provides a formalization of the school timetable to incorporate the needs of the children and adults. This approach uses a binary variable to manage the constraints of the school timetable. The school timetable is generated based on the features of the input data.

Inspired by the stable, one-legged walking platform known as a monopod, this study focuses on producing monopod-like locomotion using soft robots. Specifically, we analyze a single-legged, toe-tipped soft biped featuring two four-chambered toes. Through numerical simulation, it was demonstrated that a soft robot successfully mimics the principles of a conventional hard-mounted monopod, capable of achieving rapid and highly stable single-foot hops across various simulated conditions—whether the toe rests on the forward support foot or the head contacts the ground. This research also evaluates how this specific design adapts to unsolid or loose surfaces, such as sand, by modeling the sand as time-independent, compressive-only, and viscous-deformation materials using the viscoplastic constitutive equation. Based on these simulations, we propose adding external damping to enhance stability during hopping on soft grounds. Our simulation findings confirm that the damped bipedal soft-robot is able to maintain balance and stability while hopping on these yielding surfaces.

Over the past ten years, the Internet of Things has expanded significantly, with billions of devices currently active. Among the dominant IoT architectures is the Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) mesh approach, where nodes autonomously discover one another and establish resilient routing paths to transmit data. Operating firmware updates across these vast IoT ecosystems remains a persistent challenge. This paper presents the first extensive evaluation of firmware distribution within an operational environment using a large-scale mesh network. We demonstrate that traditional methods relying on centralized point-to-point links are unfeasible for large-scale deployments due to significant overhead from network management protocols. Instead, we assessed a novel approach leveraging automatic peer-to-peer links created via mesh protocols. Results indicate that while mesh networking successfully reduces load on the central server, end-to end delivery times remain largely unchanged. Furthermore, we identified that current end-to-end delivery mechanisms cause substantial memory leaks, compromising the reliability of devices with constrained resources. We offer concrete recommendations to resolve these issues, noting that potential improvements require further standardization efforts.

Interactive Bayes Adaptive Clinical Trial Design (BACTD) represents an innovative statistical framework designed to maximize information acquisition within a predetermined finite interaction sequence by employing an exploration-exploitation strategy. This work focuses specifically on optimizing such designs when multiple targets must be addressed simultaneously, offering a novel budget-constraint algorithm built on the principles of Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) and Tree-structured Bandits for these multi-objective scenarios. To evaluate performance, simulations utilize synthetic data configurations—both with linear and non-linear relationships—across varying dimensions and quantities of targets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms conventional sequential approaches by effectively maximizing information yield across all designated goals while adhering strictly to limited interaction budgets.

Generative-adversarial training has emerged as a potent paradigm for enhancing the robustness of deep learning models. This work introduces a framework for generating global adversarial examples specifically for quantum classifiers, utilizing the GABAT (Global Adversarial Boosting Adversarial Training) approach. Unlike the proposed method, current techniques for generating quantum adversarial instances are confined to the binary classification domain. The study evaluates the two primary categories of such instances: global adversarial instances, which possess a new label distinct from the original, and global adversarial disturbances, which maintain the original label but introduce perturbations. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework is versatile, capable of handling multiple quantum machine learning algorithms, including the Support Quantum Classifier and quantum-based neural networks.

Compliance constitutes a central aspect of contemporary security and risk governance, serving as a key indicator of risk and enabler of automated response. Although prior research has extensively examined response mechanisms based on inflexions (ixalignments) and postfix alignments within system traces, the application of these approaches to compliance verification remains underdeveloped. This paper advances the field by introducing Compliance Verification via Trace Segment Alignment (CVTSA), representing the pioneering exploration of using infix and postfix alignments for this specific purpose. CVTSA leverages existing alignment techniques by defining compliance as the detection of forbidden trace segments and categorizing these segments by the subtypes of alignments that compose them. To achieve this, the proposal integrates a novel variant of infix alignment effectively for forbidden segment verification, refining postfix alignment methodologies to manage segments composed solely of postfix matches, and outlining a framework for representing compliance rules. Furthermore, an automated process is established for generating equivalent-compliance equivalent-compliance compliance rules.

This study introduces a new model for single-cellular signal propagation, powered by a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN). Leveraging readily available Geographic Information Systems (GIS) data, the framework predicts received signal strength (RSS) with just knowledge of prior signals and cell tower locations. The model demonstrates robust generalization across expansive areas requiring no site-specific training data. When benchmarked against propagation models standardized by the 3GPP for land scenarios, the proposed method significantly outshines competitors in both rural settings. Additionally, the research offers theoretical insights into how deep learning can optimize the design of future communication systems.

This work introduces a semantics for a temporal planning language form of which we demonstrate that, under our specific constraints, finite-valued, executable plans can be formally confirmed as correct based on the given specifications. Our approach addresses three critical areas: (1) the definition of temporal Plan Unit, (2) the establishment of a language specifically tailored for describing them, and (3) the development of a method to formally validate these plans. Our approach is inspired by the Temporal Plan Specification Language (TPL), yet we have designed these solutions to be more readily implementable in software. Our definition of a plan, though more general than the traditional concept, encompasses the traditional definition as a specific instance. Our proposed language design, while more constrained than TPL in scope, allows for greater expressiveness within those limits to formally describe a broader array of temporal behaviors. Finally, our technique for a formally confirming these plans is an adaptation of existing techniques, specifically those used to verify the correctness of non-temporal plans.

We present a new methodological approach for expanding power capacity grids, driven by the response function of the network. The primary objective of model generation is to meet demand at the lowest possible total cost, encompassing the sale of electricity, installation of new grid infrastructure, and the operation and maintenance of existing infrastructure. The primary decision variables governing the existing infrastructure are investment choices in the expansion of current grid components. The model is validated using a case study based on the Nordic power grid structure, with particular attention to how the model reacts to the responsiveness introduced within the framework.

This paper examines a class of Vlasov-Poisson-like systems constrained within a finite bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, featuring reflective boundaries where particles revert upon impact. Leveraging a deterministic approach, the study establishes the existence of global-in-time weak solutions that remain regular indefinitely. Specifically, it proves the non-existence of closed trapped trajectories and implements a boundary reflection strategy when trajectories nearly encounter $\partial\Omega$. Under the premise that $\Omega$ is of class $C^{2,2}$, the work further demonstrates long-term stability and spatial uniformity.

Locating a visual phrase within an image presents significant challenges due to natural visual variation and the difficulty of defining these views algorithmically. Concept Search addresses this by shifting the focus from locating exact pixel-level matches to identifying semantically equivalent views of the query visual. A pivotal component in realizing this approach is a precise algorithm for detecting relevant text within user visual inputs. We introduce a novel method for extracting meaningful data from inputs to establish semantic links to the query visual, termed **S**earch **T**erm **I**nformation **R**etrieVAL (**S.T.R.I.C.T**). Unlike prior techniques that attempt direct optical character recognition to extract words, our approach circumvents the need to explicitly parse individual characters. Instead, it targets broader, information-rich entities to enhance the potential for semantic association.

In our framework, all available visual and textual information within an image is extracted to construct a comprehensive graph that facilitates further processing. We subsequently identify optimal entry points into this visual dependency network by comparing it with externally sourced image-text databases. These highly informative semantic access portals serve as anchors to initiate a breadth-first traversal, effectively pinpointing pertinent visual dependencies essential for accurate concept localization.

Experimental validation confirms the efficacy of our technique, demonstrating substantial gains in both extracting relevant data and identifying appropriate concept matches when compared against current state-of-the-art solutions.

Colloidal gels, characterized by a dynamic yet robust network structure, exhibit a dramatic increase in viscoelasticity upon gelation, shifting from a liquid-like to a solid-like response. This transition is often accompanied by a significant, time-dependent sol-to-gel transformation in rheological behavior. We present a method to modulate and control these rheological attributes of thermally driven gels through high-intensity, focused acoustic waves. This approach enables the non-invasive, directionally-dependent adjustment of a gel's mechanical and flow properties by applying vibrations of varying amplitude and frequency. We demonstrate an experimentally realized system where such acoustic control allows for the non-contact increase of a polymer's molecular weight, or sol-to-gel transition, and simultaneously reduces a gel's yield stress and viscosity via a process called "rheo-acoustic" shearing. This innovation establishes a new avenue for manipulating the flow dynamics within existing gel systems.

Document search, information retrieval, and related tasks within the STEM domain are heavily dependent on accurately categorizing STEM content. To address this, the author introduces a method to differentiate between two prevalent document types in STEM literature: those featuring mathematical formulas and those containing verbal descriptions of math concepts. While both types often coexist in printed and digital STEM materials, prior research has struggled to effectively distinguish them. The proposed solution centers on extracting entities from the full-text content, specifically targeting the distinct characteristics of each category. By analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of these entities to create a "mathematical-clanguage" feature, the approach successfully trains a classifier that achieves 96% accuracy in categorizing mixed documents. Consequently, this feature significantly outperforms previous methods that rely solely on part-of-speech (POS) tagging, which yielded only 76% accuracy.

In this work, we introduce a novel objective known as the Stable Pairing Problem (SPP). While market designers have recently focused heavily on the Stable Marriage Problem (SMP) and its variants to create stable rankings among participants, the SPP extends this framework to the general graph setting, where edges represent mutual proposals and bidirectional preferences may exist. The primary challenge arises because the input graph may contain stable pairings that do not align in inclusion, meaning one does not necessarily supersede the other in completeness. The central goal is thus to identify a stable subset of relationships. We demonstrate that the SPP remains essential for practical applications such as the dating industry and labor markets, illustrating that even the simplified linear ordering scenario inherently constitutes an SPP instance. Our formal analysis reveals that SPP lies within complexity class NP, is closely related to the Maximum Matching Problem (MMP), and generalizes finding the most inclusive stable set in SMPs. Notably, we prove that computing the maximum cardinal stable pairing requires solving a Hamiltonian cycle, a known NP-hard problem. Consequently, the optimization variant of SPP faces intractability. In contrast, a polynomial-time algorithm exists for determining a maximal stable pairing. Finally, we establish that the decision variant of SPP is also NP-hard.

Summary evaluation is a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) aimed at scoring the quality of generated summaries. Existing metrics predominantly rely on pre-trained models trained on summary-specific datasets, which often yield unsatisfactory assessment accuracy. This research introduces Summary Score (SumScore), a novel, thorough metric leveraged by the Cross-Encoder all-pairs classification approach combined with multiple feature representations. SumScore integrates three established scores—GloBoT, ReadabilityScore, and ScoreR, which evaluate the global meaning, sentence-readability, and coreferences within a text—alongside two new, summary-specific scores derived from the model. These represent a Structure Score, calculated using a graph-based feature, and Content Score, derived from textual entailment representations. Empirical results across five datasets validate SumScore as the most reliable summary evaluation metric to date.

We study a model designed to restore both quadratic and linear signals within a sparse framework. This task arises frequently in neurophysiology when reconstructing sparse neuronal firing rates from population activity and sparse mixtures in signal processing when recovering sparse sources from their observations. The key distinction between the scenarios lies in the non-negativity constraints applied to sparsity in the quadratic case, which renders traditional theoretical insights and algorithms developed for quadratic recovery on unconstrained datasets largely inapplicable. This research addresses these challenges by analyzing a quadratic recovery task for positive sparse sources subject to noisy observations and establishing the precise conditions required for successful reconstruction via convex optimization with an exact oracle. We further propose and analyze a practical optimization routine that incorporates approximate oracle capabilities to facilitate feasible computations. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the theoretical hypotheses and empirically demonstrate the advantages of incorporating quadratic structure into reconstruction methodologies.

Although 3D object detection in autonomous driving has advanced significantly, most recent approaches are heavily tuned, with many failing to match LiDAR-only baselines after integrating camera inputs. To address this, we present BEVFusion, a lightweight yet powerful 3D object detection framework that efficiently integrates multi-view camera and LiDAR data. The approach features a unified 3D embedding space for multi-sensor fusion, a unified multi-view query mechanism, and a streamlined network architecture designed for high efficiency. Notably, BEVFusion avoids using complex and costly components like LiDAR-camera alignment, additional embeddings, or attention modules, and it does not require applying camera parameters to LiDAR features. When benchmarked on the KITTI dataset, BEVFusion surpasses previous multi-sensor fusion techniques and reaches the top performance level within the DETECTORS category. The implementation and code are publicly available at the specified repository.

This study investigates thermal dissipation range liquid turbulence, focusing on the mechanisms by which heat is removed from the system by thermal disturbances. Our analysis employs direct numerical simulations (DNS) of water within the temperature interval of 20°C to 80°C to examine how heat transfer evolves as viscosity decreases and energy dissipation per unit volume increases under locally isotropic conditions. Consistent with prior research, the system is characterized using a non-dimensional Nusselt number. As anticipated, the Nusselt number exhibits an increasing dependency on the Reynolds number. Our numerical data aligns well with existing empirical and phenomenological models, and the effect of temperature on both the viscosity and the Nusselt number is assessed. Furthermore, this is the first numerical simulation to explicitly model molecular transport in the temperature range of 20°C to 80°C, allowing for a direct comparison with phenomenological theories. Our results confirm that the Nusselt number scales with the square root of the Reynolds number, a relationship that matches the limit predicted by the phenomenological theory of Gotoh and Thiele.

This study presents a numerical simulation of the laser-induced thermal distribution within a liquid medium to explain the complex diffraction patterns generated by the laser beam's self-induced effects. By leveraging the strong coupling between light and heat, the work utilizes a time- and space-resolved approach to compute both temperature and refractive index variations across the beam's cross-section at specific instants post-irradiation.

Design dialogues within the context of computer assisted surface modeling are frequently explored through the lens of data mining and natural language processing. However, the vast majority of existing studies lack robustness because the proposed methods often fail to be verified by independent assessments. To address this gap, we introduce Concept of Robustness (CoRe) specifically for design dialogues, utilizing an original framework of Robustness Analysis (RAnD). Applying CoRe, we evaluated over 1,000 studies and identified numerous analyses that required re-evaluation. We then conducted a comprehensive evaluation of previously reported analyses that had undergone this re-assessment. In total, the RAnD approach encompasses over 200 distinct robustness analyses, each grounded in a rigorous and comprehensive methodology.

This study introduces H-STREAM, a new research engine designed to manage vast datasets by unifying a stream processing model with the historical data capabilities of data cubes. H-STREAM integrates the Stream Management System (SMS) with the Hadoop framework and utilizes the RDBMS as the foundation for the data cube. This architecture supports the creation of streaming analytics pipelines capable of processing continuous data flows over the extensive historical records stored in Hadoop. The paper outlines the H-STREAM engine, its main components, and the mechanisms for model transformation that enable the deployment of workflows as analytics pipelines. Furthermore, the paper addresses the engineering challenges of pipeline construction within this environment and presents performance evaluations that validate the engine's efficiency, particularly in scenarios involving the processing of large data streams against the Hadoop-based data cubes.

Scholarly papers are typically evaluated based on citation counts; however, we offer an alternative metric grounded in venue status. Our methodology replaces the traditional use of paper counts with paper velocity scores for conferences, which better accounts for changing trends. Specifically, we apply discrete-time environmental modeling to derive our venue dynamic replacement metric using observed data shifts. Empirical findings demonstrate a strong positive correlation between observed and predicted performance trends across diverse venues, validating the accuracy of this approach. Consequently, this evidence supports our conclusion that venue performance can be effectively tracked using these calculated metrics, which serve as a robust substitute for citation analysis.

This work investigates a control framework designed to handle the concurrent safety verification and validation of a finite set of feedforward neural networks (NNs) within a dynamic environment. In this setting, a controller must ensure that the resulting feedback law guarantees that all NN outputs remain within predefined bounds under uncertainty, without the need for the network's underlying algebraic structure. For the special case of feedforward networks featuring ReLU activations and finite dimensions, the problem is addressed by converting the feedback bounds check into a infinite-dimensional semi-definite program (SDP). A finite-dimensional SDP approximation of this formulation is then employed to synthesize the controller. Furthermore, the approach establishes SDP conditions that simultaneously synthesize the feedback gains and the neural architecture itself.

This paper introduces a new approach to performing groupings based on a similarity matrix by ensuring an early-defined hierarchical structure within a selected cluster subset by selecting elements that define the overall grouping design. We propose a new optimization problem, solving this problem using a variant algorithmic procedure named the functorial optimization problem, which is NP-hard in nature. We then develop a heuristic multi-functional hierarchical grouping procedure (FHGO) to solve this problem, demonstrating that the objective function remains functorial in nature with respect to the objective function. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of the F-HG-O method through a comprehensive study using data from multiple datasets.

Restoring large-scale 2D image data from streaming streams is critical for many real-world applications. This paper introduces a new method that treats restoration tasks using tensor rings enhanced with adaptive patch monitoring. First, a core model representing the two-dimensional data stream is constructed as a tensor ring thread. Then, block-wise monitoring tracks the dynamic evolution within these tensor rings to guide restoration. Finally, local smoothing is applied to generate the restored output. Numerical results demonstrate superior restoration performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods in two-dimensional streaming scenarios.

Predicting future entities within Knowledge Graphs (KGs) represents a significant area of research driven by applications in reasoning tasks and knowledge acquisition. While existing methods primarily focus on dynamic KGs, this study highlights the importance of static framework exploitation, arguing that structural characteristics and temporal entity relationships in static graphs play a pivotal role in forecasting new links. Consequently, we introduce a novel predictive method designed specifically for static frameworks. Initial experiments on standard synthetic datasets, such as CW2D and CW3D, demonstrate the utility of static data for link forecasting. However, the primary contribution involves a new predictive approach that integrates graph neural networks (GNNs) with a dynamic embedding of virtual neighbors. Specifically, this method processes static data by embedding all neighbors and their temporal attributes as dynamic representations. Empirical evaluations across three real-world industrial datasets confirm that the proposed approach surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving performance gains of 10% to over 30%.

Optical resonators are essential components ultrafast oscillators, supporting self-pinned solitons that lock mode due to the balance between dispersion and nonlinear effects. These solitons remain stable only if intracavity nonlinearities are managed appropriately; in Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLM), this requirement is met by aligning the aperturing effect of the Kerr-focusing lens with the pump focus. This work conducts a geometric study of the dynamics leading to and sustaining the KLM process. We establish that a stable limit cycle emerges when the nonlinear phase shift is much less than $\pi$, driven and sustained by two mechanisms: first, the attraction toward an "equilibrium" ellipticity caused by the alignment of focusing, and second, a "repulsion" from extreme ellipticity arising when the nonlinear induced Kerr lens becomes increasingly steeply curved as it is pushed further from the flat-parabolic base state. We also present a graphical framework rooted in this equilibrium concept to assess and optimize the KLM mechanism in oscillators. Additionally, we examine how losses impact the equilibrium state and assess the soliton's stability under the influence of non-linearities that do not follow this simple model. We further illustrate through simulations that the system naturally converges to configurations optimizing the available Kerr-lensing performance.

This study investigates asynchronous online federated learning (LOFL) for nonlinear regression tasks involving a non-input feature, focusing on the distinct characteristics of this architecture. To address these nuances, we introduce a nonlinear regression LOFL framework tailored to specific non-linearity demands and analyze its convergence rates. Additionally, we account for heterogeneous computational and communication resources, as well as real-world network constraints such as packet loss and unstable bandwidth, which we model using a Markov chain. Within this setting, we propose a resource-aware asynchronous LOFL algorithm incorporating noise resampling to mitigate packet loss and adaptive bandwidth adjustment. The method also includes a theoretical convergence rate analysis. Extensive experiments using a nonlinear regression task and a bandwidth allocation system demonstrate that the algorithm achieves superior performance and generalization compared to synchronous online LOFL and other asynchronous variants, exhibiting significant gains in a time-constrained, unstable network environment by leveraging the benefits of lossy transmission.

Silicon-on-insulator membranes are widely used in various optical and optoelectronic devices. However, their minimal thickness inherently restricts optical absorption, creating a challenge for integrating active optoelectronic components like photodetectors and modulators. This limitation can be alleviated by employing these membranes as optics in the near-infrared spectrum when equipped with reflective structures that generate a photonic band gap (PBG). This work outlines the design, fabrication, and characterization of such Si-on-insulator membranes, featuring periodic aluminum-oxide ridges on the rear surface to function as mirrors. The P-band gap is designed to reflect the membrane, effectively recycling photons for multiple passes and thereby enhancing overall absorption. Additionally, P-band gap formation is expected to amplify the resonance effects of microcavities formed between the membrane and the mirror. Experimental results confirm that the membrane's resonance response in both transmission and reflection is well-matched to the intended design. Furthermore, optical measurements demonstrate a substantial boost in absorption, particularly in the resonance region, for membranes as thin as 200 nm.

Link forecasting aims to predict potential links in networks and is widely employed across various network analysis tasks. Although node embedding methods based on Random Walks (NW) are popular for this forecasting, they typically struggle with accuracy in sparse networks, where the absence of edges makes the random walk process inherently challenging. To address this limitation, this paper introduces Sparse Semantic Network Embedding (SSNE), a method that facilitates efficient and precise link prediction in sparse settings. By leveraging both existing links and the structural features of the network, we construct a semantic representation that yields compact node representations. To enhance the robustness of the embedding process, we devise an edge sampling strategy that selectively incorporates non-adjacent nodes based on the probabilistic likelihood of a link. To ensure robustness against variations, we develop a bidirectional Skip-One strategy to mitigate class imbalance caused by the scarcity of link pairs. To maintain computational efficiency, we design a message-passing mechanism that allows the model to learn latent information from neighboring embeddings rather than processing the full network. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world sparse networks demonstrate that SSNE significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art link forecasting methods.

Visible light and infrared thermal imaging serve as primary modalities for detecting and monitoring forest fires. Although existing visual and deep learning-driven fusion techniques exist, no prior frameworks specifically combine these modalities for wild fire scenarios. This study introduces FIRe-GAN, a sophisticated fusion methodology utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate visible-like imagery from infrared input for wild fire imagery. FIRe-GAN operates in two phases: initially, it utilizes a pre-trained fire detector to assess the confidence of infrared images, subsequently employing GAN-based fusion during the second phase to translate these images into a visible spectrum based on their confidence levels. Agent-based systems face challenges when dealing with an uncertain future, where future rewards may be misaligned with current preferences. This paper addresses the issue of preference–reward misalignment within the framework of hedging theory. We introduce a novel approach that combines Bellman depth with hedging mechanisms to generate Bellman-based policies. Unlike previous models that focus on the immediate next state, our algorithm evaluates preferences across an entire trajectory, effectively decoupling current actions from immediate current preferences. Additionally, the method incorporates a future-looking discount factor, which smooths discrepancies in the evaluation process. We demonstrate that this approach is not only robust to errors inherent in the Bellman update mechanism but also demonstrates that Bellman-depth strategies are powerful even when the hedging term is set to zero. Empirical results show that our algorithm is highly effective at mitigating reward preference misalignment.

Sequential recommenders are widely adopted in numerous applications. However, existing models typically fail to address the specific motivations behind a user's actions, and even when doing so, they often only capture the user's desire for recent, minimal, or local preferences. To better understand these drivers and enhance recommendation quality, this paper introduces a new method for encoding a user's motivation model based on a hidden state. By utilizing a self-attention mechanism, the proposed Hidden User Motivation Modeling (HUM) approach captures the temporal dependencies within a user's action history. We have integrated the HUM module into a standard sequential recommender system and validated the results across multiple datasets. Our results demonstrate that the integration effectively encodes distinct user motivations and significantly boosts the performance of the sequential recommender.

We also show a relationship connecting the two forms to the Bessel function through a limiting process involving a scaling limit.

This research investigates decentralized control architectures specifically tailored for linear multi-channel systems. We introduce both state-feedback and output-feedback designs that leverage a state-space system decomposition known as the High-Gain Multichannel Form (H-MCF). We demonstrate that these decentralized structures maintain computational efficiency and support plug-and-play flexibility when the number of subsystems is large. Furthermore, a new distributed control method is proposed using a design framework rooted in linear matrix inequalities (LMIs). We establish LMI-based and linear time-invariant conditions regarding closed-loop stability by analyzing the system's specific properties. Finally, we validate this approach using a case study involving the distributed state regulation of a 100-mass mechanical system, demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

Driven by the urgent necessity for effective management of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, we introduce an automatic categorization system for news articles. This work addresses two distinct classification tasks: first, detecting whether an article contains information regarding the virus, and second, identifying if the content pertains to infections, cures, or virus developments. Consequently, we introduce a new dataset comprising over 115,000 English news articles and develop a dual-stage fine-tuned model that leverages the attributes of pre-trained BERT. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we released the entire dataset and source code via GitHub to support further research.

Within the academic community, no formal consensus exists on how to classify networks; instead, a fragmented landscape of diverse concepts and methodologies prevails, often remaining inaccessible to scholars entering the field. Designed as a structured learning path, it offers a systematic approach to building network research expertise. A key innovation of this model is its integration of theoretical knowledge with practical application, linking specific methodological techniques directly to foundational theories. By mapping a researcher's progression from novice to expert, the paper also provides conceptual and technical overviews of networks from beginner through advanced levels. While extensive research has elucidated eco-evolutionary dynamics over evolutionary periods, contemporary systems often evolve rapidly enough to demand daily monitoring. These emerging, short-term scenarios challenge us to develop robust methods for characterizing their trajectories, necessitating a clear framework for analyzing the interactions between ecological and evolutionary timescales. To address this gap, we introduce a novel model that captures the non-linear feedback loops between evolution and ecology, incorporating a stochastic element to evaluate the impact of environmental variability. By varying key parameters, we demonstrate how the cadence of oscillations shifts, revealing that eco-evolutionary cycles can persist over millions of years. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions that stabilize these cycles, highlighting the significance and timing of such interactions. Importantly, these long-lasting patterns indicate that monitoring these short-term dynamics can yield critical insights into historical processes. Ultimately, the insights derived from our modeling approach hold significant promise for interpreting both ancient ecological records and predicting future system behavior.

Building large-scale speech representations has become a critical research area, driven by the widespread availability of data and the advancement of deep learning models for speech processing. Building on this, self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a leading paradigm in speech representation engineering. In this work, the authors introduce the first investigation into the robustness characteristics of self-supervised speech models. Specifically, they examine susceptibility across three key phases: pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference. Our analysis reveals that while self-supervised learning models are generally more robust during the fine-tuning stage compared to standard supervised classification, they remain significantly vulnerable during both the pre-training and inference stages. Consequently, this susceptibility can lead to poor automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance. To address these issues, the authors propose the "Speech Model Audit," a framework for evaluating model reliability, which helps identify the root causes of SSL model failures and guides researchers in developing more dependable solutions.

Decentralized, blockchain-powered platforms offer users the ability to transact directly, eliminating intermediaries and allowing the blockchain to serve as an immutable record for all exchanges. These systems generally consist of an immutable ledger, decentralized identifiers, and tokens used for value transfer. While current decentralized applications (dApps) are still in early development, their architecture supports rapid innovation and deployment. This study aims to survey the landscape of existing decentralized marketplaces, surveying their utilities and development progress. We provide a detailed breakdown of the top 50 most active dApps within this sector. Furthermore, we analyze these sites based on their utility and sector classification while highlighting their inherent risks and challenges to underscore their present vulnerabilities. This work seeks to empower researchers and practitioners in building more secure and practical decentralized marketplaces for the future by offering comprehensive insights into this evolving field.

Missing data poses a significant hurdle when analyzing clinical trial outcomes, yet traditional approaches to handling these gaps often implicitly assume that study results are free from bias—a stance that feels contradictory within this very context. Consequently, researchers require a standardized method to assess how robust their conclusions remain under plausible scenarios where effect sizes are distorted by missingness. This exam seeks to adapt the e-value, a technique originally designed for selective reporting analysis in the context of sensitivity to such missingness. The e-value acts as a unified metric of robustness by identifying the minimally justifiable statistical significance that could exist in a dataset; higher e-value magnitudes indicate greater vulnerability to bias. Demonstrating the method, we apply this logic to a study evaluating the clinical benefits of a new medication.

This study introduces a set-valued part-of-usage (POS) tagging framework designed for historic, non-current domain languages. Using these values, a SetNet network learns to forecast the appropriate collection of POS tags for each token. Experiments conducted across four distinct but historically significant POS standards covering Old Norse, Middle Dutch, and Middle French—along with a single training set utilizing Modern German as a baseline—indicate that these estimated confidence scores effectively align with their ground truth frequencies. Furthermore, strategic fusion methods significantly elevated the precision of fully labeled sequences compared to the individual capabilities of any single model. Ultimately, this demonstrates the viability of this set-valued prediction system even when training data originates from modern languages alone.

A fundamental challenge in probability and mathematical finance involves determining when a family of probability measures is integrable with respect to some governing parameter. While classical results regarding uniform integrability (UI) and regularity for signed measures, developed by researchers such as de Finetti, Dubins-Freedman, and Yoeurp, rely on the total variation norm, these approaches fail for the vast majority of practical applications. This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the integrability of both positive and signed measures. Our approach utilizes a non-uniform integrability (NUUI) condition, which is both necessary and sufficient to ensure the almost sure convergence of corresponding densities. We provide multiple equivalent characterizations of this new NUUI property and demonstrate that the resulting conditions are significantly less restrictive than traditional requirements. Notably, we prove that the classical UI condition is merely a specific subset of a broader family of sufficient criteria, all described by our NUIs condition. Finally, we illustrate the practical application of this new framework within a financial context.

Image analysis is a cornerstone of digital medicine, a field marked by a long-standing imperative for robust data standards to facilitate exchange and reuse. We believe *Highdicom* empowers a wide range of researchers working in medical imaging to fully leverage established clinical infrastructure and promote the seamless sharing of both data and software within the clinical environment.

Although numerous studies have focused on identifying specific genetic mutations linked to diseases, the majority of the genetic code remains unexplained. In this work, we introduce a technique to extract patterns from DNA sequences without any prior knowledge or specific tasks. Unlike traditional methods that typically rely on fixed positional encoding (k-mer representation), we utilize variable positional encoding (n-mer) alongside an optimized embedding strategy. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to remain generalizable across genes and organisms without requiring any form of parameter fine-tuning. We demonstrate that the resulting patterns remain consistent regardless of the encoding width used and remain undisturbed even when targeting subsets of the genome. Furthermore, these generated representations align closely with biological processes, biochemistry, and genetic knowledge. We validate this method's utility by highlighting patterns linked to gene regulation, replication, and transcription, as well as showing its capacity to detect mutation-induced modifications. Finally, these patterns exhibit a high degree of similarity to those discovered in prior research that employed supervised learning techniques.

Screening forces, which are repulsive in nature, occur when a particle inserts itself between two other particles that are attracting each other, thereby diminishing the force experienced. This screening effect is fundamental to systems where attractive interactions dominate, such as those involving liquid drops held together by surface tension or magnets aligned in parallel. While screening has been extensively studied in repulsive regimes, its role in attractive liquid-liquid systems has been less well understood, though recent experiments on frictionless liquid drops demonstrated a surprising mechanism where the screening force grows stronger as particles approach one another. This observed behavior contradicts standard screening models derived from mean-field theories and has been labeled "anomalous screening." In this work, we validate these anomalous screening forces by developing both a theoretical framework and computational simulation techniques tailored for strongly attractive forces, specifically examining how they vary with orientation. By comparing our simulations with experimental data, we confirm the existence of anomalous screening and establish that it arises from a balance between surface tension and disjoining pressure forces acting upon the interface between liquid drops.

Traditionally, crystal temperature has served as a surrogate for these complex phenomena; however, this study introduces dephasing time measurements as a direct diagnostic for addressing crystal warmth in trapped-ion platforms. By performing dephasing time measurements under varied heating conditions in a single-species two-dimensional ion ensemble, the results demonstrate the emergence of multiple heating regimes. Furthermore, the authors detail dephasing trajectories in both heating and dephasing time as indicators of the motional state distributions arising from different heating approaches. Finally, the authors outline a strategy for minimizing dephasing caused by crystal warmth through optical cooling targeting specific crystal configurations in the quantum limit. This work underscores the critical necessity of minimizing dephasing in conjunction with controlling crystal warmth to achieve the high dephasing time thresholds required for future integrated quantum information systems.

Terahertz and Edge-Roughness Spectroscopy (TERS) represents a cutting-edge technique that merges the high spatial precision of optical imaging, derived from scanning the light scattering off an AFM tip, with the deep subdiffraction field confinement provided by plasmonics. This synthesis enables the investigation of physical processes at sub-1-nm scales. Our methodology offers a fully quantum mechanical framework to calculate the total, localized electric field within the AFM tip, explicitly accounting for both short-range chemical interactions and long-range electromagnetic effects. To achieve this, we utilize the time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) approach to model the coupled dynamics of light-matter interaction and electron movement. This study demonstrates that the detailed electronic configuration of the tip's outermost atomic shell is critical for determining the induced electric field. Consequently, the distinct variations in the outer atomic arrangement between metallic and semiconducting/insulating graphene edges result in significantly different charge-field distributions across the tips. This comprehensive quantum approach facilitates the development of optimized TERS probes tailored for specific targets, while also providing a robust tool for interpreting experimental data.

Reinforcement learning theories describe how the human midbrain encloses dopamine signals representing reward prediction errors to direct goal-directed behaviors. Yet, neural decoding of these signals remains elusive, partly because it is unclear if a unified parietal signal encodes a singular learned value or a complex array of strategic values. To address this, we executed a study involving 15 participants equipped with intracranial electrodes who performed a two-action, two-reward reinforcement learning task ranging from a quick but small reward to a slower, larger one. This design compelled agents to balance exploration versus exploitation and select between immediate gains and delayed, larger payouts. Using model-based reinforcement learning fits, we identified distinct neural encoding targets across the parietal lobe: some corresponded to specific action values, others to the chosen action's expected rewards, prediction errors, or a mixture thereof. We discovered that suboptimal performance strategies were associated with the encoding of specific action values, whereas characteristic optimal strategies were linked to encoding specific reward values and prediction errors. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of these encoding targets varied across the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, midbrain area, and midbrain area, aligning with findings from non-human primate studies. Ultimately, these results underscore the essential role of diverse reinforcement learning strategies in understanding human dopamine-driven learning processes.

We introduce a method for quantifying entanglement and discussing the contextuality of $E_8$ lattice systems when they are complexified. Using complex $E_8$ lattices, we construct two equivalents: a qubit system and a fermionic model featuring extended symmetries within the context of anyonic models. For the qubit system, we calculate the entanglement via von Neumann entropy and establish contextuality through Wigner-Heywood criteria; subsequent calculations reveal that entanglement and contextuality are tied to the system's topological features. Furthermore, the associated fermionic model is linked to quantum Hall systems, thereby connecting the concepts of entanglement, contextuality, and topological order.

Monitoring time series streams for proximity is a critical challenge in data science. The concept of the Fréchet distance provides an intuitive framework for quantifying the similarity between time series, although computational demands restrict its practical utility. To address this, researchers have developed hash-based methods that map temporal series into a searchable close neighbor domain by approximating the Fréchet distance. However, existing guarantees on false positives and estimated close neighbors are overly loose. This paper establishes theoretical bounds that are substantially tighter, advancing existing understanding of accuracy in Fréchet distance approximation and directly enhancing current state-of-the-art results.

Algorithms designed to optimize high-stakes decisions face significant challenges from measurement noise, which distorts the information used for resolution. Conventional approaches to mitigating this issue rely on aggregating data from numerous, independent trials. However, this requirement can be impractical due to constraints on time or the difficulty of ensuring statistical independence. We present an alternative solution through iterative error reduction specifically tailored to this scenario. Our method models both noisy observations and the target, slightly noisy, underlying "clean" landscape via Bayesian distributions. By iteratively refining the probability density function representing the clean landscape, the algorithm drives down measurement error without necessitating the runs of numerous, unrelated experiments. Simulations demonstrate that iteratively unmasks this cleaner landscape and performs comparably to strategies employing thousands of independent tests.

This study addresses how robot standards can be effectively implemented within real-world systems. We introduce a framework designed to evaluate multiple autonomy strategies and shared autonomy schemes, with a specific focus on learning-based approaches. We demonstrate the application of this framework in the context of shared autonomy for parking, using a parking robot as an example. While parking serves as our test case, the proposed solution is applicable to a broader range of standards. The results indicate that a transition to shared autonomy enhances overall profitability, and notably, the training costs associated with broader robotics standards are significantly minimized.

Robotic navigation in unfamiliar environments remains a significant hurdle, particularly when relying on grid representations like occupancy maps that demand extensive prior knowledge of the room layout. To address this, we introduce HiTMap, a hierarchical topological map designed to represent layouts topologically rather than through a grid. HiTMap offers a computationally efficient method for both extracting and generating these representations. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating HiTMap as an additional input improves the performance of a reinforcement learning-based navigation system. Furthermore, we explore the utility of HiTMap in representing multi-story buildings, comparing our approach against an alternative hierarchical topological map framework based on existing literature.

The ADMM method is shown to converge under mild conditions. The algorithm is implemented with a generic X-ray spectrum and tested on synthetic data with additive Gaussian noise. Time series visualization plays a critical role in exploring data across science and industry. Historically, enabling users to analyze time series required proficiency with the system's interactive features, multivariate datasets made this even more demanding. Consequently, designing interactive visualizations that accommodate complex time series datasets is a significant design and algorithmic challenge. To address this, we present a new framework that enables seamless interaction between small-matrix multivariate time series sequences and longitudinal information. At the heart of this approach is a newly developed algorithm specifically crafted to map interactive cues effectively. We have integrated this algorithm into "Anima," a user-friendly system that allows both novices and experts to leverage its capabilities. Through a case study focused on oceanographic data collection, we assessed Anima's utility in supporting data analysis workflows. Our findings indicate that the system serves as an effective tool for visualizing intricate multivariate time series sequences and long-term contextual information.

Digital Health (DH) records are gaining traction as a vital tool for advancing patient care and health research, though their unstructured nature and inherent complexity hinder effective access and analysis. While many machine learning (ML) approaches have been developed to address these challenges, their utility is often restricted to specific tasks or particular data formats. By leveraging multiple similarity metrics, DSOREN successfully establishes connections between various forms of unstructured data, demonstrating that the generated embeddings are highly effective. The outcomes of this study, which were validated using two distinct DH record datasets, indicate that the model significantly outperforms existing methods in similarity assessment tasks.

Next-generation mobile communication networks must accommodate growing user demands for high-speed, low-latency, and energy-efficient data transmission. To achieve this, collaborative network coding (CNC) is proposed to enhance transmission efficiency by enabling network nodes to jointly encode and transmit data. However, optimal relay selection alongside precise relaying protocols remains a significant challenge due to the high energy consumption associated with relaying operations. This paper introduces a novel low-latency CNC framework that jointly optimizes relay assignment, active relay quantities, and power allocation to significantly cut down on relaying-related energy usage. The core of the proposal is a dual-level architecture designed for both open and closed service scenarios. In the open scenario, users are supported by multiple relays, which minimizes power consumption through a convex optimization-based allocation strategy. Conversely, the closed scenario restricts relaying choices exclusively to relays assigned by a specific user, facilitating an efficient local transmission strategy well-suited for energy-constrained, user-centric networks.

We present computational results concerning the magnetic proximity effect around a Mn monomer or dimer situated on a Niobium (110) surface. The analysis relies on the relativistic initial principles theory of Yu--Shiba--Rusin (YSR) states proposed in reference [1], utilizing a $d$-orbital model for the Mn atom and a tight-binding approach for the Nb substrate. Our calculations reveal an isotropic YSR state near the Fermi level surrounding the Mn monomer, exhibiting substantial spectral weight suppressed by the magnetic proximity effect around that system. Conversely, the anisotropic YSR states identified within the Mn dimer demonstrate higher spectral weight. Upon increasing the coupling between the Mn impurity and Nb host, both states are expected to intensify. Furthermore, the anisotropic YSR states detected in the dimer are attributed to the anisotropic nature of the $\pi$-bonding charge distribution inherent to the dimer structure.

This study details the investigation into the rare decay $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ using the technique of decay-in-flight. Data were gathered via the Suda Collaboration's CERN Proton Synchrotron, employing the two-horn focusing neutrino beam apparatus at an intensity of $1.8\times10^{11}$ protons per pulse and a frequency of $10.4\,\mathrm{Hz}$, while monitoring for the signal at a distance of 159 meters from the production point. The analysis leverages a $1.35\times10^{14}$ accumulated protons-on-target dataset to determine an initial upper limit for the decay rate, resulting in $\Gamma(\mathrm{K}^+\rightarrow\mathrm{pi}^+\mathrm{n}\bar{\mathrm{n}}) < 5.3\times10^{-12}$ (with a 90\% confidence level). The present investigation represents the inaugural experimental attempt in the realm of rare $\mathrm{K}^+\rightarrow\mathrm{pi}^+\mathrm{n}\bar{\mathrm{n}}$\ ' decay investigations through the methodology of in-flight decay.

Prejudice in the form of local minima frequently hinders robust performance in standard NCC-based distribution-to-distribution scan matching (SMM) for high-surface-finish parts, particularly in high-noise scenarios. This issue stems primarily from the excessive smoothness inherent to standard cross-correlation. This paper presents a novel NCC-based SMM utilizing a deep neural network (DNN) filter applied to the correlation function. Trained on synthetic and genuine noisy, non-rigidly aligned inputs, this approach leverages the DNN's capacity to learn that features in specific domains do not align, thereby effectively reducing the impact of surface micro-defects. Furthermore, the method integrates an optimization framework that explicitly accounts for both the correlation function and prior estimates derived from previous iterations. Experimental results across synthetic and actual noisy, non-rigidly aligned inputs confirm that applying the DNN filter significantly reduces mismatch rates and enhances overall scan matching reliability.

In the realm of image processing, edge detection is vital for identifying boundaries between different regions. Typically, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are employed for this purpose, though they demand extensive training with specific datasets. In contrast, this paper introduces a non-learning-based method designed to locate edges in satellite imagery. We also present a quantitative method for automatically selecting network parameters, removing the necessity for fine-tuning or training data. Quantitative evaluation against state-of-the-art approaches is provided, demonstrating the proposed approach's competitiveness within satellite image processing.

This study presents a new Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to mitigate such attacks. By integrating generated adversarial examples into the training process, unsupervised deep neural networks achieve enhanced resilience without relying on data augmentation. To address computational limitations, the protocol utilizes an encoder-decoder architecture that mandates minimal memory resources. Experimental evaluations across three distinct superimposed carrier systems confirm that this method surpasses existing solutions, particularly in scenarios constrained by hardware limitations.
