Recently, deep learning has markedly improved accuracy in this area, though most label sets have been developed using annotated MRI scans. Given that MRI data varies significantly across different clinics due to differences in scanning protocols, there is a risk of performance degradation when a model trained on diverse data performs poorly on clinics not represented during training. This study investigates the effectiveness of Continual Learning (CL) for multiple Sclerosis MRI segmentation, aiming to accumulate experience incrementally across four distinct clinics while maintaining strong prior performance. Intrigued by the inquiry into how dynamical systems facilitate machine intelligence, this paper posits that a system's dynamical behavior is fundamentally linked to a higher-level machine intelligence capable of detecting its own modeling errors. To elucidate this concept, we propose a framework where a primary dynamical system, representing the physical reality or "true" state, is approximated by a secondary intelligent system. When the most intelligent modeling deviates from the ideal, a frustating discrepancy emerges; this mistake is not static but evolves dynamically. We construct a coupled set of equations that integrate the original system with this temporal evolution of the error. The solution demonstrates two key properties: the coupled stable equilibrium corresponds precisely to the global attractor of the initial physical system, whereas a divergent solution (blowing up in finite time) signifies and predicts inevitable real-world system failure. Thus, the study of these coupled dynamics effectively encapsels the study of the primary dynamical system and the machine intelligence that generates it.

The Dragon Infrared Dark Nebula (DIN) is a massive, dense molecular cloud situated in Perseus, where a process of star formation is currently underway. Previous research has identified a compact infrared bright source at the cloud's core, which is currently being investigated. Our study utilizes new ALMA 1.2 mm continuum data to analyze the cloud's core, revealing a complex environment of compact emission alongside a large outflow extending approximately 0.5 pc. This outflow is primarily driven by a bright CO outflowing jet located at the center. We further observe that the core is heated by a 0.05 pc-wide plume of EMR. Based on these findings, a scenario is proposed where a low-mass outflowing object (likely a protostar) once triggered a phase of high density, leading to the current density increase. This object may have been a protostar that either grew to a high mass, accreted a large envelope of dust and gas, or both effects occurred. Furthermore, a second jet is suggested to be present at the core's center. This study supports the hypothesis that a low-mass object initiated a massive star's formation by creating a high-density core, aligning with observations of massive star formation processes.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) have recently gained significant interest as a candidate for dark matter, and simulations utilizing a modified post-newtonian (NMPy) expansion for dark matter are proving effective. This study details the implementation and execution of such a simulation, where the evolution of PBHs is treated as a cosmological fluid and its higher-order moments are tracked. We also examine the feasibility of these objects constituting dark energy. Based on these findings, an alternative hypothesis is proposed, positing that in the early universe PBHs acted as dark energy, transitioning later to a dark matter role. We further evaluate if this scenario can resolve the Hubble tension.

Systematic investigations into the mechanical and structural properties were conducted on models consisting of chains of rigid wedges arranged in a flat standing position. These systems were constructed using chains built from either triangular or trapezoidal components. The chains were subjected to controlled compression and decompression under vertical loading, with the resulting chain configurations, combined with three-dimensional motion data for every chain element, recorded and studied to understand the resulting dynamic and structural changes within the chains when these external forces were altered in intensity. The generated chain configurations demonstrate multiple different stages, including the existence of stages with the splay arrangement of every single chain element. The formation process of stages with splay arrangement in these chains is studied and demonstrated both numerically and experimentally using physical models. The physical models were constructed using 3D printed elements and used for the physical model validation and stages formation demonstration process described in this work.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks, yet modifying these pre-trained models is typically difficult due to their size; however, reducing this barrier is crucial. Previous attempts at unique-token adaptation, which aligns pre-trained LEMs with specific task-related identifiers, have been limited by the use of only singular or limited sets of such identifiers. We introduce a novel method that extends this approach by learning distinct, class-specific tokens for semantic classification. We evaluated this method on the coarse-grained classification task defined by HuggingFace's NLP leader board, focusing on 12 categories. We utilized the RoBERTa model adapted via this technique using data from the test set for fine-taining, despite such data access being unusual practice during the initial evaluation. We observed that the number of fine-tuned tokens per class significantly impacts the model's performance. We further demonstrated that the proposed technique is effective when applied using just a small sample randomly selected from the entire domain set for a given classification. We also proved that the distinct tokens generated by the model are statistically and functionally reliable. We further confirmed that this efficient framework can leverage diverse pre-trained architectures with strong results across a broad spectrum of tasks.

This paper addresses three main issues: first, the conditions under which adding elements creates problems in preference ordering; second, the challenges arising in adding new preferrred items; and third, adding items that are neutral. We present two new findings regarding these problems. First, we show that if preferences over pairs satisfy the weak contraction condition proposed by Mas-Colell, we can derive preference structure for groups of any size. Second, we prove Mas-Colell's strict convexity model leads to a loss of contrast between small groups and the risk function used in preference-based social choice. We also illustrate this contrast using the risk function used in Mas-Colell's work.

Traditional approaches largely treat these domains separately, although recent studies on supercooled liquids have identified significant crossovers within their temperature-dependent behavior. Notably, these liquids undergo a shift from an Arrhenius to a Vogel-Fulcher-Hammel-Tang (VFHT)–like temperature profile as they approach the glass transition, suggesting that their specific heat ($C_p$) and viscosity ($\eta$) are intrinsically linked through the VFH specific heat equation expressed as $\eta \propto \exp[(\Delta H/T)\cdot C_p]$. By analyzing a broad spectrum of polymer rheology and calorimetry data, the study confirms this VFH-based VFH thermodynamic-dynamic connection exists specifically for glass-forming liquids that exhibit an "A-type" transition in their calorimetry signal during the glass transition. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that both polymers and inorganic glass formers share a "B-type" thermodynamic-dynamic profile, distinct from systems classified as type-A.

Denial of a process represents a key mechanism in human psychological development, where a person rejects aspects of reality to cope with trauma or distress. In the realm of NLP, it is proposed that such denial can be modeled as information suppression. If topics deemed difficult or repulsive need to be set aside, they must be obscured from view during the context of their removal. To study this, we introduce a *denial process* designed for transformer models, enabling them to hide specific content while still generating text. Unlike traditional methods that merely filter words by probability, our approach suppresses them by storing the hidden content in internal states and obscuring it from the output. Utilizing a parameter called the "denial level" allows us to control the extent of this suppression. The results indicate an intricate relationship where increasing suppression initially boosts perplexity, but further suppression eventually improves it, suggesting that optimal internal hidden representations differ from those of standard self-attention mechanisms, which often rely on global visibility. Moreover, when examining the suppression of words belonging to distinct semantic categories, the data reveals that highly correlated terms are more likely to be hidden together in denial states compared to those with low correlations. Finally, we observe that these denial states filter out content based on its nature; specifically, words with negative connotations are more frequently suppressed than positive ones, and the model demonstrates an ability to grasp the nuances of context.

In machine translation workflows look-ahead prediction is often overlooked despite its effectiveness in research settings. This is primarily due to the high computational costs associated with implementing it in real-time production environments. This paper demonstrates that looking-ahead attention mechanisms can still be successfully deployed at scale, provided that correct system architecture choices and optimization strategies are utilized. Furthermore, we investigate source-language-aware decoding, another research-only NMT technique previously untested in industrial applications. Our results show that both methods significantly improve translation quality at the sentence level without incurring substantial delays or memory overheads in production systems, all while maintaining cost-efficiency.

We investigate large-$N$ CFTs where CFTs interact locally through gauge-theory-like mechanisms. The discovery of metastable Neel-type magnetic skyrmions has generated significant interest in their technological applications. This study examines the magnetic behavior of the multicomponent compound Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, characterized by neel-type skyrmions situated in a hexagonal lattice. We reveal that, in contrast to systems where Neel-type lattices form without crystals lacking magnetically inactive atoms, the exchange-driven melting in this specific crystal lattice does not follow the Boltzmann distribution. This atypical behavior stems from the crystallographic anisotropy, and we conclude that the anisotropy of the magnetization is tactically controlled to manipulate the melting dynamics of the metastable magnetical textures.

The mean-field framework is widely regarded as the primary method for modeling the impact of small-scale turbulent motions on global dynamos. Our findings indicate that employing the complete set of mean-field terms yields results that align with the convection parameters studied. This success validates the mean-field framework as a reliable tool for analyzing small-scale turbulence effects in global dynamos, provided that only $K$ is not used in isolation but the full spectrum of turbulent influences is incorporated.

Securing high-quality data annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTF) for natural language tasks like text summarization is notoriously difficult due to the "needles in a haystack" challenge: top-tier samples are scarce within the vast, heterogeneous worker pool. This paper introduces a novel methodology to identify exceptional talent by analyzing TMT orders through a game-theoretic framework. We model the interaction between workers seeking strategies to select orders yielding the highest monetary reward and requesters designing tasks to prevent exploitation, a dynamic that enables a focus on summarization where we determine optimal pricing policies. These policies dictate reward structures based on specific project attributes, such as attribute counts and complexity, to select ideal candidates. We also examine the impact of these mechanisms on workforce demographics, worker retention, and the cost of annotation, offering practical guidance for SL systems aiming to locate expert annotators efficiently on MTC.

Text-video retrieval (TVR) involves locating relevant, semantically aligned videos from an extensive repository given a specific query. This is a demanding task, as it requires processing high-capacity video sequences and complex natural language while simultaneously extracting a fine-grained association between textual details and visual content. To address these challenges, we introduce Token Shift-Select-NeT (TS2-Net), a lightweight yet effective lightweight encoder-decoder framework designed to enhance TVR. We hypothesize that employing separate sub-encoding streams for text and video coupled with an innovative dual-phase mechanism can facilitate more precise alignments. We further leverage hierarchical token shift strategies to promote long-range dependency modeling, ensuring that distant contextual signals are maintained. Additionally, we incorporate a novel dual-routing mechanism designed to boost the efficiency and scalability of large-scale video indexing systems. Extensive experimental results across two major benchmarks demonstrate that TS2-Net outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements in retrieval accuracy by increasing area under the curve.

This study examines, for the first time, neutral currents in the top quark sector that alter particle flavour, specifically through $Z$ boson couplings connecting different generations ($s \to c$, $b \to s$, and $t \to c$ via a NLO SM baseline). We employ a simplified model framework to constrain these non-standard neutral processes using precision electroweak data, focusing on the three key observables: $F_{\text{ew}}$, $\Delta\rho$, and $S$. Our analysis reveals that the most stringent limits arise from the $W$ mass and $F_{\text{ew}}$ measurements, whereas the $Z$-pole coupling constraints remain the most sensitive for directly limiting $F_{\text{ew}}$. We further investigate the implications of these findings within the framework of Effective Field Theory (EFT), considering their potential impact on top quark decays involving a $Z$ boson. Additionally, we assess whether these new flavour-violating neutral currents could explain the ALICE collaboration's observation of an excess yield in the charm quark spectrum within the jet-jet event topology at the ALICE detector.

Artificial intelligence (AI) represents a transformative and rapidly evolving field within computer science, characterized by significant innovation and substantial growth in related literature. However, these publications frequently focus solely on specific technologies and underlying methodologies, often neglecting critical insights into potential future research trajectories. Given that definitions vary among diverse stakeholders with varying viewpoints, addressing this gap requires a systematic effort to create a refined conceptual framework for artificial intelligence. This effort necessitates a sound modeling approach grounded in established conceptualization techniques. Consequently, this work introduces a structured refinement of artificial intelligence as a concept, outlining a clear map of its conceptual components. As an initial step in this endeavor, we generate three distinct meta-arguments derived from published research, demonstrating diverse perspectives on what constitutes artificial intelligence.

This kernel framework is engineered to align the resulting GP functions with established mathematical invariance principles found in transformational systems, such as spatial, temporal, or complex invariance. To demonstrate their practical application, this proposed kernel structure is integrated into the design of the K-Net architecture, a kernel-based neural network. This architecture maps functions across multiple output spaces by sequentially processing them through a sequence of Gaussian processes. We evaluate this framework through the design of kernels for visual tasks targeting spatial and temporal invariance, specifically utilizing benchmark datasets from machine learning for invariance and reinforcement learning for testing. This work advances the customization of Gaussian process architectures to explicitly incorporate prior mathematical knowledge about unknown regression behaviors.

Deep representations have established themselves as the top-tier methods for various tasks, including image recognition, classification, and retrieval. However, optimizing these representations for complex, multi-objective goals remains difficult, often resulting in suboptimal outcomes when relying on standard training metrics. This paper introduces a novel dual-network architecture specifically engineered to learn deep representations that excel at complex tasks. This approach leverages Sinkhorn divergence as an optimal descriptor, enabling effective training objectives. By employing this methodology to retrain two widely used networks—the Visual Generative Encoder for image search and a model for multi-way search—we demonstrate significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art methods.

Between November 2020 and January 2021, the United Kingdom implemented the country's most expansive digital contact tracing initiative to date. This program integrated data from local public health bodies, private sector entities, and the mobile telecommunications industry. Our study examines the specific influence of local agency participation on COVID-19 detection within contact networks, analyzing the role of localized collaboration using weekly contact and infection data across 130 UK locations spanning December 2020 to January 2021. By modeling the temporal lag between contacts and cases, along with the volume of notifications sent by the government's app, we employed Bayesian additive regression tree models to evaluate the impact of local partnerships on disease identification. The findings indicate that app users residing in towns with active local partnerships experienced a 16% higher likelihood of COVID-19 detection compared to those in towns without them, even after accounting for user demographics. These results suggest that local collaboration significantly enhances the efficacy of digital contact tracing efforts.

Additionally, the work applies isochrone fitting to derive an estimated age of roughly 1.25 billion years and determines a reddening value ($R_V A_G$) of 0.144. We address robot calibration by training a neural network to automatically adjust camera-in-hand extrinsic parameters from an image containing four visible features. By incorporating intrinsic parameters and the eye-to-hand transformation as additional inputs, the network regains the eye-to-hand movement for a given camera image when estimated jointly with intrinsic information. Since no labeled adjustments are employed during network training, this approach leverages unsupervised learning to perform the prediction step entirely autonomously. Consequently, only manual annotation of the four 3D world coordinates for each image is required for the system setup. We further develop an iterative method that refines both camera intrinsics and the eye-to-hand matrix by repeatedly forward-passing a network whose output includes previously estimated hand poses as new inputs. Extensive experiments confirm that our model effectively predicts camera-in-hand poses with high accuracy and robustness across various viewpoints and under differing lighting conditions when four feature points are visible.

We introduce Reverse Constrained Training (RCT), a universal framework that streamlines model training by automatically selecting the most promising constraint from a set of candidates. RCT is built on two key components: first, a weighting function that adjusts sampling probabilities to prioritize states near the current trajectory, and second, a selection mechanism that chooses constraints based on their performance. Unlike other methods, RCT requires no tuning of hyperparameters, allowing it to handle both continuous and discrete action spaces and support any policy constraint formulation. Extensive testing demonstrates that RCT significantly boosts sample efficiency and final performance across diverse tasks, including those with difficult constraints, while also reducing the time needed to reach target reward levels. https://github.com/google-research/reversely-constrained-training.

GAIA is an ESA mission dedicated to creating an all-sky census of stellar and sub-stellar bodies, extending to the 25th magnitude in the G band, with the primary goal of generating comprehensive 3D galactic maps. The instrument utilizes a dual-aperture optical system featuring two co-aligned, wide-field cameras designed to capture precise photometric and astrometric data. To support these objectives, GAIA employs the Differential Charge-Coupled Sensor (DCCS) technology, specifically the 100 x 100 element DCS sensor, which delivers exceptional performance. The GAI A instrument further includes a high-precision radial velocity photometer designed to measure line-of-sight velocities for stars brighter than 14th magnitude. The GAIA Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC) delivers the data products derived from the mission's observations. This document outlines the scientific objectives, instrument specifications, and a detailed account of the on-board and down-earth processing strategies used within the mission framework.

In the realm of graph algorithms, bag-width-ordered treewidth decompositions are widely regarded as valuable, as many problem solutions can be adapted to run in time dependent on this width plus the bag size. While previous efficient linear-time decompositions existed only for pathwidth and vertex separation, this paper introduces new approaches for treewidth that introduce bag-sized subproblems known as "vertex dividers." Specifically, we present two innovations: first, the Compact Vertex Divider, which has bag sizes matching the input vertex order, and second, the Multi-Factorized Compact Vertex Divider (MCDV), where bag sizes correspond to the arities of multiple vertex separators. Both techniques achieve linear time construction and facilitate solutions to numerous problems in time $f(k,n)$, with $k$ being not just the standard treewidth but also the multi-fold vertex fold (MVF)—a newly defined parameter representing the minimum bag size across a collection of $k$ vertex divider sequences. Notably, the MVF is a strict lower bound on the standard vertex fold, and its associated problems can be solved efficiently when $k$ is fixed. Empirical results indicate that the MVVF often offers a significantly tighter bound than traditional vertex separation, leading to substantially faster solution times. Additionally, the paper details methods for adapting standard-treewidth decomposition into those using bag-sized vertex dividers, a modification proven empirically to accelerate solutions for several key graph problems.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) integrate physical laws as constraints within a machine learning architecture, enabling the resolution of intricate differential equations across fields like fluid dynamics and quantum mechanics. Nevertheless, because PINNs rely fundamentally on optimization-based stochastic gradient descent, their outputs often remain uncertain. This study introduces "authorized machine learning," a novel framework that combines traditional numerical methods with PINNs to construct reliable bounds for PINN predictions. The core concept involves identifying specific output intervals where physical constraints are strictly honored and estimating these permissions regions through a customized error estimator. Experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively balances accuracy and computational feasibility, offering guaranteed bounds for approximating complex fluid flows.

A key challenge in researching airborne pathogens is accurately modeling the spatial distribution of air pollution, which serves as a primary influence on respiratory and infectious disease outcomes. This paper introduces a new method for modeling the location-based spread of airborne contaminants by integrating geostatistics with machine learning and "neural network" systems. These models are built upon empirical data collected from ground monitoring stations and aerial pollution maps, utilizing deep learning techniques such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to capture complex patterns within imagery and time-series data. The proposed framework was tested using Smallpox virus concentration data gathered from various urban centers to assess its predictive capabilities for airborne pathogens. The study demonstrates that the combined approach significantly enhances the precision of modeling atmospheric pollution spread, offering a robust tool for analyzing the propagation of contagious viruses in the air and predicting future disease trends based on environmental factors.

We examine the bandit framework where each arm offers a vector of features, and pulling one yields a scalar reward resulting from a linear interaction between these vectors and a hidden parameter vector. We analyze two distinct scenarios: where a set of a priori known arms is available, and where the agent may either choose an arm from a pre-defined pool or, if a subset of arms is available, select them directly.

Notably, in cases where a smaller pool of arms is provided, we find that learning the parameter vector faces substantial challenges due to potential sparsity in features and limited arms, potentially rendering precise recovery infeasible. In response, we propose a new method that leverages current arm-specific features and accumulated reward data to generate arm-specific pseudo-labels. This approach enables the use of the arm-specific pseudo-labels and reward history to estimate the unknown parameters. We provide theoretical guarantees for this estimator, proving that the estimation error is well-controlled under the assumption that arms are sufficiently diverse. We also present a practical algorithm for generating arm-specific pseudo-labels and show that this method is effective in cases where arms are not diverse. We provide numerical results to support the proposed method.

A significant challenge in machine learning is that a small fraction of data can severely degrade model performance. This paper investigates how such data contamination impacts Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We analyze the training dynamics of GNNs in contaminated settings and establish theoretical bounds to explain why they are more susceptible to corruption compared to standard multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). Furthermore, we explain why GNNs often fail to generalize to unseen nodes despite achieving low training error. To address this, we introduce a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based approach to detect irregular data patterns, which experimentally demonstrates enhanced generalization capabilities over basic MLNs. Finally, we validate our findings empirically across various node classification benchmarks using publicly available datasets.

The primary function of astrometric catalogs is to establish links between catalogs and to derive astrometric solutions. However, astrometric data proves less effective for the initial catalog matching stage, as it lacks the photometric characteristics that significantly aid in identifying sources. In this paper, photometric parameters are integrated into astrometric catalogs to facilitate cross-matching. A new matching approach leverages photometric similarity alongside position. Additionally, a revised version of the 2MASS catalog matching algorithm employs a multi-level weighting strategy that prioritizes source color consistency alongside spatial coordinates. This updated version achieves higher precision and efficiency compared to the original algorithm. The paper further introduces a catalog enhancement to increase the source recovery rate; this method utilizes flux-limited subsamples to mitigate the bias caused by sky brightness limits. Testing with an incomplete version of the catalog confirms that both strategies are successful, demonstrating that photometric parameters are a valuable asset in catalog cross-identification.

In  [i]infinite hypergraph theory[/i], a novel variant of the classic [i]minimum edge cover problem[/i] is introduced. A subset $F$ of hyperedges is designated a [i]minimal edge cover[/i] if it is a covering set, yet the removal of any single edge from it destroys the property of being a covering set. While finite hypergraphs possess unique minimal edge covers, this uniqueness generally fails when dealing with infinite ones. The primary focus of this framework involves characterizing minimal edge covers in infinite hypergraphs, specifically establishing that the minimal edges in this context fall into two distinct categories: those that function identically to minimal edge sets in equivalent edge graphs and those representing a newly defined class characteristic to infinite structures. This study also presents an algorithm with a time complexity of $O(|E|+|V|)$ for enumerating the minimal edges across any given infinite hypergraph. Furthermore, the framework explores the relationship between minimal edge covers and the fundamental problem of minimum edge cover decomposition. Finally, this work investigates questions concerning the count of minimal edge covers found within random hypergraphs generated using the Erdős–Rényi model.

Ontologies serve as a standardized method for explicitly defining data semantics, making them crucial for exchange and interpretation across systems. However, this explicit definition results in extensive networks of formal relationships that present a major obstacle: visualizing these relationships becomes increasingly difficult as their scale and complexity grow beyond manageable limits. While the literature currently offers several visualization strategies for browsing large ontologies, each suffers from significant flaws, such as imposing restrictive non-hierarchical assumptions or failing to scale adequately. To overcome these limitations in state-of-the-art visualization tools, we introduce **OntoPlot**, a browser-based, interactive tool that visualizes formal relationships within large-scale ontoids. Built upon the force-directed graph algorithm, OntoPlot presents the ontology structure as a dynamic spatial layout. Users can interact with the system through a range of controls that facilitate both localized and global comprehension. User testing confirms that OntoPlot is user-friendly and scales effectively to handle large volumes of ontologic data. By bridging the gap between developers and data semantics, we aim to demonstrate that OntoPlot serves as an effective tool for the collaborative development and analysis of complex ontologic definitions.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are typically trained on extensive corpora of labeled speech paired with transcripts. Yet, acquiring precise transcriptions incurs significant costs, and annotator availability is often restricted. While Transcription and Speech Annotation can be performed by experts, acquiring clean data remains costly; thus, leveraging large amounts of unlabeled speech offers a cost-effective alternative. This paper introduces a framework for building semi-supervised, end-to-end ASRs by leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled speech without incurring annotation costs. Although CycleGAN has demonstrated potential in generating synthetic transcripts from speech, applying it directly to ASR is challenging due to its reliance on cycle-consistency, which is ill-defined for the specific properties required in text generation. Instead of cycle-consistency, we introduce an adversarial loss function that effectively transforms speech waveforms into speech-labeled data through an encoder within the model; this approach, combined with the Cramer distance from optimal transport theory, provides robust discrimination. Furthermore, we incorporate a speaker invariance metric to detect domain discrepancies between synthesized transcripts and real text. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed method effectively closes the gap between domains in both clean and noisy speech conditions, achieving significant improvements in semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems compared to baselines across both clean and noisy conditions.

This study introduces a model of predictive neuroscience known as Active Inference, utilized to train a single neural network for independent robot navigation in unknown terrains. The framework demonstrates that within one architecture, crucial capabilities for non-cartesian movement can emerge, including probabilistic path pre-planning, impulse generation for translation through the environment, and optimization for minimization of prediction errors relative to internal neural maps. By formulating neural representations via unit bi-axes or non-Cartesian orientations, the approach enables robust robotic motion. Training the system involves modeling sensory inputs and latent states from simulated sensor readings and comparing simulated outputs against target results. The experiment was conducted using a simulated three-dimensional physical robot equipped with a 360-degree laser range finder. Additionally, the architecture handles uncertainties inherent in both robotic dynamics and the sensing mechanisms to facilitate superior real-world generalization. Ultimately, this study underscores the potential of the Active Inference framework to explain various aspects of biological intelligence while delivering high-performance robotic solutions.

A theoretical investigation into the origin of the Soret effect within binary mixtures of soft molecules reveals, via molecular dynamics simulations and analytical calculations, that molecular free movement significantly influences both mechanisms and mathematical descriptions of this phenomenon. Specifically, even when individual molecular correlations are negligible, the transport of heat and matter remains strongly regulated by the transport of their respective movements and their combined effects.

Building on established DREAM challenges, this study introduces two evaluations of language models in generative grammar instruction following and generation. The first task involves generating a set of sentences in response to a prompt, which requires adhering to specific constraints outlined within them. The second task involves generating a sentence that describes the input. Both tasks require following specific grammatical rules provided in the input, which are often implicit and require inference capabilities from the input, making these two evaluation benchmarks challenging yet valuable measures for generative language models.

Pedestrian identification (PI) is a critical technology for intelligent transportation and public security. Its effectiveness depends on accurately matching the same individual across images taken in different environments. A significant limitation of current PI models is their tendency to generate false positives (FPs) and low ranks when the image pair comes from dissimilar domains. To address this, we introduce an unsupervised, false-positive targeting re-rank strategy. Our method first filters out obvious FPs by discarding pairs with highly dissimilar image features. For the remaining ambiguous cases, we design a "box refinement" approach that iteratively updates the images' bounding boxes to extract the most discriminative facial or body features, thereby confirming or retaining FPs based on the final similarity scores. Consequently, these suspected FPs are then properly ordered by the model. Extensive tests on two major public benchmarks, PEID and PRW, confirm that our method outperforms existing solutions, achieving a significant reduction in FP rates without requiring any new training.

Neural machine translation relies on sequence-to-sequence frameworks that leverage attention mechanisms to facilitate translation. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to explicitly incorporate rich linguistic knowledge, such as the hierarchical tree syntax of language and its relational features. Although various studies have addressed this limitation by introducing syntactic constraints or features to enhance translation quality at the cost of slower processing speeds, there remains a lack of sequence-to-tree decoding methods capable of integrating both syntax and parsing information. Addressing this gap, this work introduces a novel method called "syntactic linking," which combines parsing and translation in a single top-down tree structure. By utilizing the parse tree to define valid building blocks and their order while syntactic links account for non-local dependencies, the decoding process translates sentences into structured forms respecting syntactic rules. Experiments on the English-FTS dataset and the WMT19 German-FTS dataset demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art results in both quality and speed compared to prior art. Specifically, this method improves FTS translation scores by 0.73 BLEU points and reduces processing time by 3.5 times relative to the previous best approach.

Accurate binding energies are essential for comprehensively understanding interstellar molecules, and since these values cannot be measured in astrochemical environments, they must be estimated using terrestrial quantum chemistry techniques. However, numerous factors are used to evaluate the reliability of binding energies, creating a significant hurdle for researchers selecting suitable methods. To address this, we have developed a Binding Energy Assessment (BEA) database that contains binding energies derived from 16 different quantum chemistry approaches ranging widely, from semi-empirical methods to highly accurate coupled-cluster models. These values were systematically calculated using 26 combinations of basis sets and model corrections. By analyzing the deviations between these binding energy estimates and the reference benchmark energies provided by BEA, users can assess the suitability of specific methods for their own research. Binding energy estimates from this database are accessible at https://bea.ubc.ca.

Neural machine translation (NMT) models are surprisingly sensitive to minor modifications, such as pruning, quantization, or retraining with limited data, which can significantly degrade their performance. To develop low-resource MT systems, researchers must optimize computational and memory usage without compromising the models' translation capabilities. We investigate the stability of NMT during post-training extraction and byte-level network quantization, specifically analyzing how these processes impact low-data regimes. We present an experimental framework that allows for the direct comparison of NMT models using either distillation or quantization under low-resource conditions. Our results demonstrate that distillation offers a robust path to creating smaller, more efficient translators capable of maintaining or improving translation performance, whereas re-practiced distilled models can sometimes surpass full NMT systems. However, we also observe that NMT models are highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices, which can lead to substantial performance drops in re-practiced scenarios. We introduce the open-source "MT-Fragility" (MFF) benchmark, a new methodology designed to assess how easily a model's performance deteriorates after extraction or modification. This tool helps researchers evaluate various extraction techniques, guiding the development of more efficient and scalable NMT architectures. To facilitate the broader adoption of distillation techniques, we have released the Byte-T (BT) distillation protocol, a straightforward retraining approach that can be applied to any model using the BT architecture.

The study introduces a hypergraph-based method for determining the Dirichlet problem solution associated with a specific nonlinear partial differential equation (P.D.E.) featuring power functions and a novel nonlinear element referred to as "the only function-graph." This function-graph is defined by the property that the sum of its inputs plus the input of their product equals their product alone ($x+y+xy$). By utilizing the Laplacian of mean-value on hypergraphs and constructing Lagrangian and Euler equations via a hypergraph density, the method is further validated through an application to the "Burgers-like" P.D.E.; notably, these derived solutions coincide exactly with those produced by traditional techniques.

Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved considerable advancements in pneumothraia segmentation within chest X-rays (CXR). Despite this, limitations in annotated data remain a significant hurdle in the development of pneumonia classifiers and lesion detectors. This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of increasing available labeled datasets through image augmentation techniques to train high-performing segmentation models. Specifically, we applied a combination of autoencoder-based augmentation and traditional strategies—including augmentation followed by aggressive cropping and traditional augmentation (rotation, color jitter, etc.)—to generate diverse variations of training images. Experimental results across multiple augmentation approaches were evaluated using classical U-Net architectures. The models trained on augmented and cropped data outperformed those relying solely on the original training set. Notably, integrating autoencoder-based augmentation with traditional strategies yielded superior outcomes compared to other configurations. These findings indicate data augmentation coupled with conventional strategies is particularly advantageous for training U-Net segmentation models on limited labeled datasets.

Although current captioning models excel at detailed captioning, they struggle to strictly adhere to specific rules when descriptions need to be regulated according to user input. Rule-following captioning is a recently proposed technique that represents a description as a pair consisting of the provided rules and the desired caption. This work investigates a two-stage training approach: first, the model is trained to generate high-quality descriptions, and second, it is adapted to effectively follow rules when given a input pair. This framework is generalized during the second phase to accept any new set of rules without further training on them. This approach leverages pre-trained models to achieve state-of-the-art performance in detailed captioning and demonstrates exceptional capability in rule-following tasks.

"We offer an expanded definition of damage to align with contemporary causal frameworks, specifically incorporating the notion of causal structures that integrate unobserved variables. By framing damage within this updated ontology, we develop a distinct, equivalent, purely causal characterization that effectively distinguishes physical objects from mere collections of energy or forces. As the resulting definition relies exclusively on established causal terminology, the task of proving its correctness can be anchored in the now-mature mathematical theory of causal models, a field that has been rigorously developed over recent years."

Although deep learning has shown remarkable success in numerous applications, conventional implementations rely on fixed, rigid designs that struggle to accommodate shifting requirements. This rigidity makes it difficult for end-users to develop new functionalities or adapt existing models to novel data and diverse demands. Consequently, this research seeks to bridge the gap by integrating the scalability and adaptability of Apache Spark with deep learning capabilities. By bridging Spark's flexibility with the power of deep learning, we aim accredit the extendability of model machine (MMLSpark), a new framework introduced here expands Spark Mllib by incorporating popular convolutional and recurrent deep learning architectures alongside adaptable measurement tools and scalable execution environments. Through MMLSpark, the convolutional deep learning modules can be readily extended to incorporate novel operations, measurement strategies, and data formats, enabling seamless adaptation to new tasks without compromising prior capabilities. Furthermore, MMLSpark facilitates easy integration of newly emerging deep learning architectures and the rapid prototyping of performance metrics. By facilitating flexible model updates, MMLSpark allows users to seamlessly adapt to new data types and evolving requirements. Complementing the MMLSpark framework performance measurement tools enable efficient, automated evaluation protocols to expedite the development and refinement of models.

Translation of speech into languages other than the original has long been a critical component of international communication, yet it remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces the Zero-shot Voice Translation (ZSVT) task, a form of speech translation where the model outputs not only the translated text but also modifies the acoustic characteristics of its source language to match the target language style. This is achieved by leveraging the linguistic and phonetic alignment capabilities of the model. We present a discrete representation for both phonetic and phonemic information to train the system. Additionally, we utilize a discrete latent space to capture target language acoustic characteristics alongside a discrete encoding module for extracting linguistic features. These two components are then integrated into an autoregressive architecture. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed ZSVT system achieves zero-shot performance that surpasses several zero-shot and fine-tuned benchmarks. We also release this system and provide comprehensive evaluation protocols for researchers.

This paper proposes a probabilistic load forecasting methodology for distribution networks. The primary methodology involves characterizing the higher-order statistical moments of the aggregate demand using univariate Wavelet Convolutional Neural Networks. The final one-hour demand forecast is generated through an integration of unsupervised techniques, such as Kernel Density Estimation. The study evaluates various network segments, specifically focusing on identifying maximum daily demand.

Although domain expertise represents a significant and potentially decisive factor in scientific discoveries and engineering advancements, it is frequently overlooked in favor of a predominant focus on data and algorithms within machine learning. Consequently, this paper investigates strategies for embedding such expertise into these models. It begins by outlining three primary challenges in expertise integration, drawing on findings from various existing and recent studies, and proceeds to construct a comprehensive blueprint for guiding future research. This blueprint employs a front-rear classification system for techniques, distinguishing between approaches that transform models into expertise-centric ones and those that analyze models from an expert's perspective, and it categorizes integration methods based on key developmental phases: pre-processing, modeling, and post-processing.

The ongoing spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has precipitated a global pandemic, characterized by an unprecedented infection toll and mortality rates that have severely strained healthcare infrastructure worldwide. While respiratory symptoms are prevalent, a pneumonia variant of the virus targets the lungs, necessitating timely diagnosis and effective treatment to curb its trajectory. Although high-resolution CT (HRCT) scans are highly effective for detecting this variant, the associated contrast enhancement required for such imaging is often unavailable in resource-limited regions. Furthermore, the scarcity of expert radiologists and pulmonologists, coupled with the immense volume of scans generated during widespread outbreaks, further complicates manual diagnosis. To address these hurdles, this study introduces the Weakly Guided Localization and Segmentation of COVID-19 (WLoSS-CL) framework, a novel method designed to localize and segment CT images of affected patients using weakly guided learning. WLoSS-CL employs an ensemble of three specialized networks: a convolutional network for anatomical localization, one for segmentation, and a third for uncertainty estimation regarding the segmentation. By utilizing an image-level labeling strategy that bypasses the need for labor-intensive pixel-level annotation, WLoSS-CL achieves competitive accuracy on both localization and segmentation tasks. Additionally, it generates reliable uncertainty maps that effectively identify uncertain segmentation outcomes. Accurate diagnosis of spinal diseases relies heavily on the localization and recognition of vertebral bodies, tasks that are prone to errors when performed manually. This study introduces a fully automated framework for localizing and recognizing vertebral bodies in CT images, grounded in 3D reconstruction, whole-spine alignment, and analysis. The method begins by reconstructing the vertebral bodies from the CT dataset and locates them using probability volume regions, resolving local ambiguities. Spinal realignment is accomplished by modeling the spine as a curve, constrained within the union of vertebral body centers from the initial localization step. The recognition process, performed on slice-level images aligned along this spine curve, employs a anatomically inspired recurrent neural network to select the correct vertebral level while simultaneously classifying it. The boundary segmentation of these reconstructed bodies is achieved through a region-saliency trained convolutional network. Furthermore, to mitigate shape irregularities, surface smoothing is executed via anatomically constrained optimization guided by sparse Gaussian fields. Finally, performance evaluations across two independent datasets demonstrate that the entire pipeline attains a mean segmentation accuracy of 90.1% and a vertebral body localization accuracy of 97.1%, achieving a recognition sensitivity of 0.91 with a 0.94 area under the curve.

We present a novel theoretical model describing the interaction of a classical electron beam with strong optical fields, resulting in what is termed resonant electron scattering. When the oscillation period of a tightly bound electron matches the incident electron's round-trip period within the interaction zone, this resonance occurs. The work includes a theoretical analysis of this resonant scattering as well as numerical simulations of standard non-resonant processes. Furthermore, the scattering cross-sections for the resonant case are compared against those of atomic resonant scattering in strong fields, such as High Harmonic Generation (HHG). Under conditions of ultrastrong field-electron coupling, the resonance exhibits dynamical stabilization, analogous to high-harmonic light scattering. Finally, the results are summarized in terms of a stability diagram, which identifies the conditions for dynamical stabilization and outlines the predicted signal spectrum of the resonant scattering.

This study introduces a new framework aimed at resolving the issue of distinguishing quantum states via a variational approach applied to state distinguishability. By employing fidelity as a measure for this distinguishability, the work derives a lower bound for the difference in state probabilities. Leveraging variational inequalities within the context of low-dimensional approximations, the author demonstrates that a greater value of fidelity corresponds to a smaller difference between quantum state probabilities, thereby establishing a clear, quantitative relationship between the two factors.

This work examines a localized tearing mechanism within slab collisionless plasmas, which operates independently of large-scale reconnection methods like magnetic reconnection driven by fast electrons. We demonstrate that in such plasmas, guided by the specific geometry of the slab, magnetic reconnection can occur on scales smaller than the initial tear mode due to the absence of electron inertia effects and the resulting modification of particle trajectories. This process is accompanied by the generation of significant induced currents and intense heating. We also explore the phenomenon in the context of current sheet reconnection occurring between two counter-flowing plasma streams, showing that it enables reconnection of initial tears on a scale comparable to the initial perturbation, which is significantly faster than the initial perturbation timescale. This enhanced rate allows for rapid energy conversion. Finally, we emphasize that this mechanism could potentially explain observations made in solar wind and magnetospheres where large-scale theories struggle to account for the observed phenomena.

Recent advancements in fashion design leverage user preferences to create bespoke garments. Our objective is to modify a user's provided image to enhance its appeal to others, noting that these desired alterations primarily occur at the feature level rather than the global appearance level. To solve this, we introduce a semi-supervised training framework alongside a perceptual loss function. This semi-supervised process utilizes image spins to generate supplementary supervision, facilitating a low-to-high resolution training transition to effectively model feature-level visual traits. Using image rotations expands the training data distribution and lowers dependence on additional samples. The proposed perceptual loss aligns structural and semantic information across source and target views to preserve crucial design elements during modification. Broadly, our approach enhances the visual traits of input images and specifically optimizes them to increase their retrieval scores. Extensive experiments confirm the efficacy of our method in both trait manipulation and fashion image retrieval tasks.

This study examines a methodology for tackling an extensive category of linear ill-posed issues within the framework of Banach spaces, drawing inspiration from dual gradient descent strategies used in machine learning. By integrating concepts dual to homogenization and standardization, a new dual standard operator has been formulated. Incorporating this operator into a general algorithm generates a family of methods designed to mitigate ill-conditioned problems. Furthermore, leveraging Enns' analysis of operator factorization, convergence results for these methods have been established. Finally, the algorithm's practicality and performance were demonstrated through its application to phase retrieval and total variation regularization tasks.

Generating synthetic training data for deep learning models often involves incorporating synthetic forces or costs. This study focuses on synthesizing occlusion maps for image expense creation. Unlike prior approaches that relied on ray casting, this paper introduces a neural network-based network for occlusion map generation. This new technique operates by estimating a low-resolution occlusion map through a convolutional neural network, which is then refined into a high-resolution map using a generative adversarial network framework employing a generator and a discriminator. Empirical evidence shows that these maps are integrated into light field depth estimation, proving that maps generated by this proposed model yield superior performance compared to those based on geometric ray tracing methods.

Using the bilinear technique, we derive new representations for a Fokas-Lenells equation. This approach not only reproduces known formulas established by Akhtariak and Bilinear through the same approach, but also generates additional instances such as the bilinear form of the bilinear formula.

We present a non-Riemannian approach to formulating Einstein's theory, grounded in a 12-dimensional frame field residing on the solution space of the integrability conditions of a generalized Levi-Civita connection. This framework utilizes double field theory, where the solution is expressed as the real part of a complex frame field, specifically addressing the solvability of Levi-Civita equation integrability. By employing the general solution, derived within this context, we construct a non-Riemannian gravitational action, effectively acting as a boundary term. Remarkably, this boundary term can be reinterpreted as the total time derivative of a vector field, effectively vanishing in the context of the action. Furthermore, this non-Riemannian framework facilitates the introduction of various torsion components, akin to Super-skew-symmetric torsion found in Supergravity, thereby opening the possibility of non-commutative and non-associative geometric structures. These findings suggest a novel pathway for formulating Supergravity, while this non-commutative Levi-Civita approach may also hold promise for applications in Quantum Gravity.

The increasing popularity of wireless Wi-Fi has surged, driven largely by its convenience and affordability, allowing users to connect to the internet from anywhere without cables even in expansive homes. However, this ubiquity has created a problem: many households deploy multiple access points (APs) to cover large areas, inadvertently causing interference among those signals. In mitigation, some also install network extenders to boost coverage, yet extenders can introduce their own interference issues. This paper introduces a model to calculate the "channel load" of neighboring APs, a feature enabled by the IEEE 802.11 standard's 802.11k (neighbor report) and 802.11v (load access network survey) specifications. Using these features, mobile client devices can gather data to decide which AP or extender offers the best connection, such as the optimal channel, while simultaneously selecting the best available service provider. The model's effectiveness in accurately locating the optimal AP or extender, especially in densely populated homes, has been validated through simulations. These simulations demonstrate that selecting the best device improves both the speed and reliability of the internet connection. The proposed mechanism is flexible enough to be integrated into various existing client architectures to enhance their performance.
